typed: The U-tube gauge is a better way of demonstrating the effect of liquid density on pressure. The original jet-distance experiment would not reliably demonstrate that difference.
phys_1_1 G6.issue: Lesson 5 had learners look for a density effect in jet distance, but jets from the same depth land together whatever the liquid; the density test now uses a simple U-tube pressure gauge Science error: learners were asked to predict and measure which liquid squirts farthest. By Torricelli's law the exit speed v = sqrt(2gh) does not depend on density, so water, salt water and oil at the same depth land at the same distance, and learners would see no difference. The pressure differences are real (rho x g x h = 1,030 x 10 x 0.10 = 1,030 Pa; 1,000 Pa; 920 Pa, recomputed) and a water U-tube would show 1,030/10,000 = 10.3 cm, 10.0 cm and 9.2 cm. The teacher decides whether a funnel, balloon rubber and clear tube are available; if not, present the table and reason from density only. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL Learners first observe that the three streams land at about the same distance (the speed of a jet depends on depth, not on density), so jets cannot show the effect of density. A simple pressure gauge (a funnel covered with thin balloon rubber, joined by a clear tube to a U-tube of coloured water) is then lowered to 10 cm in each liquid, by the teacher or one group at a time. The water in the U-tube stands highest for salt water (about 10.3 cm), lower for water (10.0 cm) and lowest for oil (9.2 cm); learners measure the differences with a ruler. typed: An engine block is a more realistic example for the 1,000 N load used in the calculations. Keep the simplified hydraulic jack figures and explain that real garage jacks use additional mechanical advantage.
phys_1_1 G8.issue: A 1,000 N load is about 100 kg, not a matatu (about 25,000 N); the jack is now shown lifting an engine block with the same numbers, and the note says real jacks use a longer handle and bigger pistons 1,000 N is the weight of about 100 kg, not of a matatu: a 14-seat matatu (Toyota HiAce type) has a gross weight of about 3 tonnes, roughly 25,000 N (checked: 2,500 kg x 10 N/kg). The classroom numbers (50 N, 5 cm2, 100 cm2, 1,000 N) are right for the physics, so they are kept and the load is renamed to something that really weighs 1,000 N (an engine block, about 100 kg). The note says a real garage jack also uses a long handle and a larger piston ratio. Teacher decides: this reframing or rescaling all numbers (for example 5 cm2 : 500 cm2 for 10,000 N). CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL lifts a heavy engine block with a small workshop hydraulic jack using only a 50 N push, yet the engine block needs 1,000 N (about 100 kg) to be lifted. A whole matatu weighs about 25,000 N, so a real garage jack also uses a long handle and a larger piston ratio; the classroom numbers are a simplified model of the same idea.

typed: Retain the vocabulary wall, sentence frames and alternative ways of explaining concepts. The teacher should confirm the Kiswahili terms with the school's Kiswahili teacher before displaying them.
phys_1_1 G9.issue: No supports for English learners or learners with special needs; added a Kiswahili word wall and sentence frame, more than one way to show the model, and a number support for the calculation lesson The sequence had no language support for English learners and no Kiswahili terms (guideline 12). Teachers must check the Kiswahili terms with local usage before they go on the wall; I could not verify them against a Kiswahili physics glossary. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL Use the name 'pressure' and no other term. Build a word wall with Kiswahili support for English learners: pressure (shinikizo), force (nguvu), area (eneo), weight (uzito); add density (msongamano), depth (kina) and atmospheric pressure (shinikizo la angahewa) when they arise. Let learners explain first in Kiswahili or their home language, then in English, with the frame 'The ___ face has a smaller area, so the pressure is ___.'
